regulations.title: Statutory basis for licensing supervised living homes

Supervised Living — Scope (24-hour facility in a home environment; licensed if serving 2+ adults or 1+ minors; 'C' designation for adults with a primary developmental disability; minors and adults may not reside together)
Supervised Living — Operations (a facility serves no more than six clients when clients have mental illness or developmental disabilities)

Physical plant: single bedrooms at least 100 sq ft, double bedrooms at least 160 sq ft, no more than two clients per bedroom; at least one full bathroom per five or fewer persons including staff and family
LME determination of need for additional supervised living beds
License fees and annual renewal. The license cannot be issued until the fee is paid; licenses expire at the end of the calendar year.
Letter of support from the LME/MCO required with a residential license application (except ICF/IID)
Operating a licensable facility without a license is a Class H felony; $1,000 per day fine

sections.executive_summary:
North Carolina licenses small group homes for adults with intellectual and developmental disabilities (I/DD) as **supervised living** facilities under G.S. 122C and 10A NCAC 27G .5600 [S1][S2]. Adult I/DD homes carry the 'C' designation (adults whose primary diagnosis is a developmental disability) [S2]. A home must be licensed if it serves two or more adults or one or more minors, and minors and adults may not live in the same facility [S2]. Operating a licensable facility without a license is a Class H felony with a $1,000-per-day fine [S4]. The licensing regulator is the DHSR Mental Health Licensure & Certification Section [S3][S5]. Homes serving clients with developmental disabilities are capped at six clients [S50], so the initial license fee is the **$350** base fee with no per-bed charge [S4].

Medicaid pays for the service, not the building. Residential Supports under the NC Innovations 1915(c) waiver is administered by the four LME/MCOs, which operate as Tailored Plans and contract with and pay providers [S8][S12][S14]. There is no public state fee schedule for it [S14]. The only rates retrieved are from Alliance Health's FY27 schedule, effective October 1, 2026: **$158.47** (Level 1), **$208.72** (Level 2), **$218.10** (Level 3) and **$228.62** (Level 4) per day, subject to LME/MCO funding [S17]. Room and board is not paid by Medicaid [S15][S16]. It is typically funded from the resident's income, and the 2026 SSI federal benefit rate is $994 per month [S24]. Since April 2026, a new Residential Supports provider must also hold one national accreditation (COA, CQL, JCAHO or CARF) before enrolling [S9].

Demand is large but slot-limited. NCDHHS counted **20,150** people on the Innovations waitlist on September 30, 2025, up from 18,457 a year earlier. Only 106 were removed in that quarter, and no new slots were approved for FY2025-26 [S48]. NCDHHS also reports that group homes are among the settings people prefer when transitioning out of institutions [S48]. None of this guarantees referrals to a new home, because homes fill through the LME/MCO choice-list process.

**The economics are thin and depend heavily on the level mix.** At Alliance's October 2026 rates, with sourced wage proxies and every cost the rules create, three 6-bed homes serving Level 2/3 residents (18 residents) earn about **$6,636 per month (5.7% margin)** at 90% occupancy. That is the profit-leading configuration. It breaks even at about **84.5%** occupancy, first turns profitable in month 8, and needs about **$408,323** of cash through the ramp-up. Two homes earn about $4,002 per month (5.1%) and one Level 2/3 home about $1,368 (3.5%). A single 4-bed home loses about $5,715 per month, and an all-Level-1 home loses about $2,771. A $1.49-per-hour higher direct-care wage erases most of the default profit (see the financial narrative). This business works only with scale, residents assigned to Level 2 or above, disciplined occupancy and an operator who keeps overhead lean.
sections.service_model:
**Who is served.** Adults with a primary developmental-disability diagnosis, who may also have other diagnoses, live in a supervised living home with the 'C' designation [S2]. Rule .5601 defines supervised living as a 24-hour facility providing residential services in a home environment [S2]. The CMS-archived State Plan language describes these homes as group homes of under seven beds [S1], and the operations rule caps homes serving people with mental illness or developmental disabilities at six clients [S50].

**Related settings that are not the model here.** An Alternative Family Living ('F') home in a private residence serves no more than three adults [S2]. NC Medicaid says an unlicensed supervised living home may serve only one adult [S15]. Manufactured or mobile homes may be used only for three or fewer residents [S5]. Residential Supports is described as supporting a person to live in a group home or an Alternative Family Living setting [S56]. This report models only licensed group homes with up to six residents.

**How the service is funded.** The Medicaid service is Residential Supports under NC Innovations (CMS waiver 0423.R04.00) [S12]. A secondary source reports the waiver was renewed for July 1, 2024 through June 30, 2029 [S13]. Per the Trillium 2026-2027 benefit plan, a member who receives Residential Supports may not receive several other waiver and State Plan services, including Home Modifications, Community Living and Supports, Supported Living and State Plan personal care [S10]. This reflects one provider delivering a whole-day residential service. The same plan limits adults in residential settings to 40 hours per week combined of community networking, day supports and supported employment [S10]. The residential provider is therefore usually not the day-program provider.

**What a customer should understand.** The license (DHSR) and the payment (LME/MCO) are separate gates. A home can be licensed and still earn nothing until an LME/MCO enrolls the provider, accreditation is complete and a resident is authorized.
sections.licensing_pathway:
The steps below follow DHSR's published process. Where sources conflict or are silent, that is stated.

1. **Form the business.** Set up an entity, and get an EIN and NCTracks-ready records. The LLC filing fee ($125) and annual report ($200, due April 15) come from secondary guides [S38][S39], and the Secretary of State fee schedule was not opened.
2. **Contact the LME/MCO in your region for a letter of support.** All residential providers except ICF/IID must obtain one to accompany the application (G.S. 122C-23.1) [S3]. LME/MCOs also determine the local need for additional supervised living beds [S51]. There are four LME/MCOs, one per county [S48].
3. **Secure the site and local zoning approval.** Residential providers need zoning approval, submitted with the application [S4]. Physical-plant rules checked in DHSR's materials:
   - single bedrooms of at least 100 sq ft and double bedrooms of at least 160 sq ft, with no more than two clients per bedroom;
   - at least one full bathroom for every five or fewer persons, counting staff and their family;
   - two remotely located exits per occupied story for facilities with 4–6 clients or two stories [S5].
4. **Submit the application packet and pay the license fee.** The initial fee is paid with the application [S6]. For a non-ICF/IID facility with 6 or fewer beds it is $350 base and $0 per bed [S4]. The license cannot be issued until the fee is paid [S6]. DHSR sends the application to its Construction Section after the packet is submitted and the fee paid [S3]. The Construction fee must be paid before review or an initial inspection [S5]. The fee table is on slide 35 ('Initial Fees') of DHSR's new-provider deck and appears to show about $225 for a 4–6 bed non-ICF/IID home. The slide image is low-resolution, so confirm the exact amount with the Construction Section Help Desk.
5. **Construction review.** DHSR's February 2026 new-provider deck says 8–10 weeks [S5], and the DHSR FAQ gives a similar figure [S4]. A code interpretation can add delay. Plan for the longer end. Construction Section help desk: (919) 855-3893 [S5].
6. **Program review.** DHSR gives the applicant six months to complete the program review. After that the application can be rescinded or denied [S3].
7. **Staff and facility ready before licensure.** All staff must be in place and the facility completely furnished and ready to open before an initial license is issued [S4]. Every staff member needs a criminal record check within 180 days of the application review [S5] and a Health Care Personnel Registry check within 90 days of the licensure review [S5]. DHSR provides no personnel training. Online-only CPR is not accepted, and medication administration training must be in person where staff store or administer medication [S5].
8. **Medicaid enrollment.** NCTracks charges a $100 NC application fee at initial enrollment and again every five years [S21][S22]. An older NCTracks guide says the fee is collected per site location, so confirm with NCTracks whether you owe it per home. NC Medicaid says a federal fee ($750 in calendar 2026) applies 'when applicable' [S21][S23]. Whether it applies to this provider type was not confirmed. A vendor blog reports clean applications cleared in about 11.76 days in June 2026 [S55]. That is a secondary figure, not a guarantee.
9. **Accreditation and LME/MCO contract.** A new Residential Supports provider must hold national accreditation before enrolling [S9]. Which accreditors are accepted for Residential Supports should be confirmed against the NCTracks Provider Permission Matrix. Providers also need an LME/MCO network contract [S8]. How the license, accreditation and contracting steps are sequenced was not documented, so confirm the order with your LME/MCO before spending on the lease.

**After licensure.** The initial license can run up to 15 months. After that, licenses are renewed annually and expire at the end of the calendar year, so the first renewal falls on the next December 31 after issuance (G.S. 122C-23(e)) [S6]. The renewal fee amount was not verified, and the model assumes it equals the $350 initial fee. A change of ownership requires 30 days' written notice from the current licensee, and the new owner may not operate until licensed [S5]. Smoking is prohibited inside licensed facilities [S5].
sections.reimbursement:
**How the money actually flows.** NC Innovations is a managed-care waiver, not fee-for-service. LME/MCOs administer the waiver services and oversee the provider network [S8]. NC Medicaid's budget notice identifies Innovations services as managed by Tailored Plans and outside the published state fee schedule [S14]. A provider therefore bills its LME/MCO under that plan's contract, using that plan's rate schedule.

**Rates retrieved (Alliance Health, FY27, effective October 1, 2026).** Residential Supports pays a per diem by level [S17]:
- Level 1 (H2016): $158.47
- Level 2 (T2014): $208.72
- Level 3 (T2020): $218.10
- Level 4 (H2016 HI): $228.62

The Alternative Family Living Level 1 rate is $161.12 [S17]. Alliance states the rates are subject to change based on LME/MCO funding [S17]. Partners, Trillium and Vaya may pay differently, and their schedules were not retrieved. The criteria for assigning residents to Levels 1–4 were not verified. Whether the $7.68 add-on below is already in the Alliance figures is unknown. An earlier 2023-era FAQ figure ($99.03/day for Level 1) was seen but is not verified as current, and is not used.

**Direct care worker (DCW) add-on.** NC Medicaid implemented incremental Innovations DCW rate increases, funded by $21.3 million in recurring state funds starting in SFY 2027 [S11]. Provider rate increases are effective October 1, 2026. The July 1, 2026 retroactivity applies to LME/MCO capitation, not to provider rates. LME/MCOs may retroactively process provider rates only back to October 1, 2026, and only after validating that the funds are used as the legislature intended [S11][S18]. No add-on revenue is modeled for July–September 2026. The uniform add-on is $0.30 per 15-minute unit [S11]. The S.L. 2026-41 code table gives Residential Supports (H2016, T2014, T2020, H2016 HI) a **$7.68 per-diem** add-on, assuming 64 units and a group size of 2.5 [S18]. Providers must file an attestation with their LME/MCO to receive it. LME/MCOs report usage to NC Medicaid [S11][S18]. The financial model does **not** add the $7.68 on top of the Alliance rates, because it is unconfirmed whether the schedule already includes it. If it is not included, it would add about $234 per resident per month (7.68 × 30.42). For 16.2 occupied beds that is about $3,800 per month, an upside to confirm in writing.

**Rate risk.** A SFY 2025-26 notice slated a 3% reduction for Tailored Plan-managed Innovations services effective October 1, 2025 [S14]. Whether it is still in effect in 2026 was not verified.

**What Medicaid does not pay.** Residential Supports payments exclude room and board [S15][S16]. Residents typically contribute from SSI (federal benefit rate $994 per month in 2026 [S24]) or earnings. The model assumes $750 per resident per month, an operator estimate that leaves about $244 for personal needs. State/County Special Assistance is a cash supplement for room and board in approved residential facilities, including group homes, for people who are 65+ or disabled [S25]. DHHS materials confirm a $1,397 monthly base rate plus a $70 personal needs allowance for 2026. The DHHS brochure says benefits go to eligible people in DHSR-licensed residential facilities, with examples that include group homes/supervised living and mental health group homes. Eligibility for each resident (age or disability, income and assets) must still be checked with the county DSS. It is not modeled, but it could raise room-and-board revenue above $750 for eligible residents.

**Waiver cost limit.** The NC Medicaid page states the Innovations annual cost cap was raised from $135,000 to $184,000 per waiver year [S8], but other passages on the same page still cite $135,000, so the cap is treated as unconfirmed. For scale, the Alliance Level 2 per diem is about $76,200 per year.
sections.demand:
**Waitlist.** NCDHHS reports 20,150 people remaining on the Innovations Waiver waitlist at September 30, 2025, up from 18,457 a year earlier. It states the list has grown [S48]. Only 106 people were removed in the July–September 2025 quarter, compared with 409 in the same period a year earlier [S48]. NCDHHS reported 14,736 approved active waiver slots, with 14,185 active slots in use and 123 reserve slots remaining. No additional slots were approved for FY2025-26 [S48]. A third-party aggregator reports 21,449 people at March 31, 2026 and a 12.26-year average wait. These are unverified against the official dashboard and are not used [S53]. NCDHHS's dashboard says it is not intended to show when individuals will receive the waiver [S49].

**Why this matters to a provider.** The waitlist shows unmet need, but a person on the list is not yet funded for Residential Supports. Funded demand comes from people already enrolled in the waiver who need a residential setting. NCDHHS's quarterly report also shows:
- Group homes and ICFs are the top settings desired by people in transition planning.
- The primary funding source for transitions is the Innovations Waiver [S48].
- 82 people with I/DD moved from institutional settings in FY25 (129 including other program data), and 24 in July–September 2025. The consent-order benchmark for the fiscal year ending June 30, 2026 is 83 [S48].
- 16 people were diverted from institutions in the quarter [S48].
- 12,386 people with I/DD received 1915(i) services in the quarter, an alternative pathway [S48].

**Supply signals.** NCDHHS states North Carolina faces a critical shortage of direct support professionals [S48]. Providers could not use 626,791 authorized CLS units in July–September 2025 because of lack of provider or staff availability (summed across the four LME/MCOs, computed from the report's values) [S48]. That is a different service from Residential Supports, but it shows staffing is the binding constraint on capacity.

**Barriers.** Guardian objections are the leading reason people do not begin transition planning, and exceptional behavioral health needs are the leading reported barrier to transition [S48]. Homes that can serve higher-need residents are therefore in demand, but those residents also carry heavier staffing costs (see the financial narrative).

**What was not found.** There was no statewide count of licensed .5600 homes, census or occupancy data, or referral-source breakdown. No source shows that a new provider receives referrals from the LME/MCO or the state. New homes fill through the choice-list process and enrollments.
sections.operations:
**Staffing rules: what was and was not verified.** The staffing rule for supervised living is 10A NCAC 27G .5602 (Staff). Paragraph (b), as quoted in a DHSR statement of deficiencies, requires at least one staff member present at all times when any adult client is on the premises, unless the client's treatment or habilitation plan documents otherwise. The modeled coverage (one awake staff around the clock plus a second staff for part of the day) meets that floor. The ratio and overnight paragraphs ((c) and (d)) were not retrieved. A 2018 DHHS report to the legislature describes at least one staff per six individuals [S52], but it is not confirmed as the current rule. The model's hours are operator estimates; read .5602 in full and check your LME/MCO's service definition before committing. Required in the sourced materials:
- Criminal record checks (within 180 days of application review) and Health Care Personnel Registry checks (within 90 days of licensure review) for every staff member [S5].
- In-person medication administration training from a qualified trainer for all staff where the facility stores or administers medication, and in-person CPR (online-only is not accepted) [S5].
- DHSR provides no personnel training, so the provider must train staff [S5].
- A qualified professional, defined by 10A NCAC 27G .0104 as a person holding a license, certificate, registration or permit from the governing board of a human service profession [S4]. Specific manager qualifications and annual training hours for supervised living homes were not verified.
- Staff in place and the home fully furnished before an initial license is issued [S4], which means paying payroll before any revenue.

**Oversight.** DHSR performs complaint resolution, annual reviews and inspections of each group home, which can lead to suspension or revocation [S7]. Inspection frequency beyond 'annual reviews' was not verified.

**Systems and compliance.**
- **EVV.** NC Medicaid requires electronic visit verification for certain HCBS including some Innovations services, and Tailored Plans (and most Standard Plans) use HHAeXchange [S19][S20]. The sources name Community Living and Supports and Supported Living, not Residential Supports. Whether Residential Supports is subject to EVV was not confirmed, so ask your LME/MCO. The model includes a per-resident records/billing software line but no separate EVV fee.
- **DCW attestation.** Providers must file an attestation with the LME/MCO to receive the DCW add-on [S11][S18] and should track how the funds are used, because LME/MCOs report usage to NC Medicaid [S11].
- **Accreditation.** Maintain national accreditation as a condition of enrollment [S9]. Providers already enrolled must re-enroll and report accreditation by April 20, 2027.
- **Billing.** Each LME/MCO has its own claims and authorization process; budget for a billing and authorizations coordinator.

**Physical plant.** Keep bedroom sizes, bathroom ratios and exits compliant [S5]. Count staff and their family toward the bathroom ratio.
sections.market_conditions:
**Pricing context.** The Medicaid per diems (Alliance, Level 1–4: $158.47 to $228.62 per day [S17]) are the realistic revenue base. Private-pay I/DD group home prices were not found. CareScout and Genworth survey assisted living communities, not I/DD group homes, and the NC medians conflict: CareScout's 2025 press-release table shows $74,400 per year [S27], a secondary guide citing CareScout shows $77,955 [S54], and Genworth's 2024 survey showed $76,245 [S29]. Those figures are context only and are not used as revenue assumptions.

**Wages.** Wage evidence is thin and mostly secondary:
- The statewide all-occupation median wage is $47,970 (May 2025) [S30].
- The Raleigh-Cary mean hourly wage is $34.01 across all occupations, with $19.29 for the personal care and service group and $16.61 for food preparation and serving [S31]. These are group-level proxies, not direct support worker figures.
- Secondary summaries citing BLS give an NC median of $38,460 for nursing assistants (about $18.49 per hour) [S32], $63,270 for LPNs [S33] and $84,350 for RNs ($40.56 per hour) [S34].
- Direct support worker, cook and manager wages for NC were not directly sourced.
- The NC minimum wage is $7.25 and local ordinances are preempted, per a secondary payroll guide [S35]. The model's $17.00 per hour is above that, but below the CNA median, so it is an optimistic assumption.

**Employer taxes.** The 2026 NC unemployment insurance taxable wage base is $34,200 and the standard new-employer rate is 1.000%. The experienced-employer maximum is 5.76% [S36][S37]. Workers' compensation class rates for residential care were not retrieved [S43].

**Real estate.** Rent for a 4–5 bedroom home is an operator estimate. Secondary rent benchmarks [S44][S45] are for small units or unclear scope and were not used. HUD's FY2026 Fair Market Rents took effect October 1, 2025 [S46], but Charlotte-area bedroom figures could not be tied to a verified table.

**Policy trend.** The 2026 appropriation adds $21.3 million in recurring state funds for Innovations DCW rate increases starting SFY 2027 [S11]. That is positive for margins, but a 3% reduction was slated in the prior budget cycle [S14], so rate direction is uncertain. The count of enrolled Residential Supports providers and licensed homes was not found, so competitive intensity cannot be quantified.
sections.financial_narrative:
**How the P&L is built.** Revenue per resident-month is the Alliance Medicaid per diem for the assumed level mix multiplied by 30.42 days, plus $750 of room and board collected from the resident [S17][S24]. For the Level 2/3 mix that is about $6,492 plus $750, or roughly **$7,242 per resident per month**, and about $117,000 per month at 90% occupancy for 18 residents. Costs are:
- direct support hours;
- a program manager/qualified professional and a billing coordinator;
- RN consultant hours;
- payroll burden of 17.8% [S36];
- rent, utilities, vehicle, insurance, accreditation and DHSR renewal, all fixed per home (vacant beds still cost rent);
- food and software, which scale with census.

Most non-wage costs are operator estimates, labeled as such in each line. No overtime or relief-coverage premium is modeled for 24/7 staffing, so actual labor cost is likely higher than shown.

**Results at 90% default occupancy (85% conservative, 95% optimistic).**

| Configuration | Net/month | Margin | Break-even occupancy | First profit month | Cash needed |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 3 homes, 18 residents, Level 2/3 | $6,636 | 5.7% | 84.5% | 8 | $408,323 |
| 2 homes, 12 residents, Level 2/3 | $4,002 | 5.1% | 85.0% | 6 | $213,726 |
| 1 home, 6 residents, Level 2/3 | $1,368 | 3.5% | 86.6% | 6 | $132,963 |
| 1 home, 6 residents, Level 3/4 | -$2,122 | -5.2% | 95.1% | none | $219,641 |
| 1 home, 6 residents, all Level 1 | -$2,771 | -9.2% | 99.1% | none | $216,990 |
| 1 home, 4 residents, all Level 2 | -$5,715 | -22.4% | 111.7% (not reachable) | none | $279,163 |

The three-home Level 2/3 configuration leads because overhead (1.5 FTE manager, 0.75 FTE billing, accreditation and accounting) is spread over 18 residents. The 4-bed home cannot break even even at full occupancy. Level 3/4 pays more per day but loses money because it assumes two awake staff around the clock. Level 1 does not cover required coverage and overhead at $158.47.

**Key sensitivities.**
1. **Wage.** The default uses $17.00 per hour, an operator estimate. The sourced proxies are higher: about $18.49 for NC nursing assistants [S32] and $19.29 for the Raleigh-Cary personal care group [S31]. At $18.49 the default three-home profit falls to about **$200 per month**, two homes lose about $300, the one-home Level 2/3 loses about $800, and the all-Level-1 home loses about $4,500 (about $7,400 for the 4-bed). A wage at or above the CNA median should be treated as the realistic planning case, and $17.00 only as a low case. The $17.00 wage clears the $7.25 minimum [S35], and no local minimum wage applies per a secondary source.
2. **Occupancy.** The default break-even is 84.5%, and the conservative case (85%) sits almost exactly at break-even, so a slow fill or empty beds between residents erases profit. Each month of slower filling adds about a month of fixed cost.
3. **Level assignment.** The model assumes Level 2/3 residents. Level definitions and assignment criteria were not verified, and the LME/MCO controls them.
4. **Rate source.** Rates are Alliance's, subject to LME/MCO funding [S17]. Another LME/MCO may pay less or more, and the status of the 3% reduction is unknown [S14].
5. **DCW add-on (upside).** If the $7.68 per day is not already in the schedule, it adds about $3,800 per month at the default configuration (about $234 per resident-month × 16.2 occupied beds) [S18]. That is more than the modeled profit. Confirm in writing whether it is already included, and file the attestation [S11][S18].
6. **Staffing hours and overtime.** The DSP hours are estimates, and the ratio and overnight paragraphs of the staffing rule were not retrieved. A higher requirement would raise costs materially, because direct support wages are the largest expense. Overtime (1.5× over 40 hours per week) or relief hours for sick and vacation coverage are not costed.

**Startup and cash.** Startup costs are lowest for one home and scale with the number of homes. They include license fees ($350 per home), accreditation ($6,000–$15,000 estimate), the $100 NC enrollment fee (possibly charged per site), a federal fee of $0–$750 that may not apply, furnishings, vehicles, deposits and pre-licensing payroll, because staff must be in place before the license is issued [S4]. The Construction review fee is modeled at about $225 per home, read from a low-resolution slide in DHSR's new-provider deck [S5]; confirm the exact amount with the Help Desk. The cash-needed figures above include the modeled ramp-up deficit. They were computed before the Construction fee and any per-site NCTracks fee were added to the startup costs, so they are slightly understated. Read them as the floor for planning, not a forecast.
sections.risks:
- **Rate and funding risk.** Rates are published by each LME/MCO and are subject to change with funding [S17]. A 3% reduction was slated in SFY 2025-26 and its current status is unverified [S14]. Rates at Partners, Trillium and Vaya were not retrieved. The DCW add-on requires attestation and use reporting [S11][S18]. Because residents are paid by level, any reclassification to a lower level cuts revenue directly.
- **Wage and workforce risk.** NCDHHS describes a critical DSP shortage [S48]. The default wage ($17.00) is below the sourced proxies ($18.49 CNA median; $19.29 Raleigh-Cary personal care group) [S31][S32]. At $18.49 the default profit falls to about $200 per month, and a metro with a higher market wage would be worse. Round-the-clock coverage also creates overtime or relief hours that the model does not cost. Turnover raises UI experience rates, which can reach 5.76% [S37].
- **Occupancy and fill risk.** Break-even occupancy is 84.5% for the default, and homes of one to two units run from 85% to over 100%. The waitlist [S48] does not mean a new home gets referrals; new homes fill through the choice-list process, and a waitlisted person is not yet funded. Guardian objections slow transitions [S48].
- **Regulatory gating risk.** The path requires an LME/MCO letter of support, local zoning, construction review of about 8–10 weeks (longer if a code interpretation is needed), a six-month program review window, accreditation and enrollment, and you must have staff and a furnished home in place before licensure [S3][S4][S5][S9]. Payroll and rent therefore run before any revenue. Working capital, not the license fee, is the real barrier.
- **Enforcement risk.** Unlicensed operation is a Class H felony with a $1,000-per-day fine [S4]. DHSR annual reviews and complaint inspections can lead to suspension or revocation [S7].
- **Unverified rule risk.** The staffing ratio and overnight paragraphs of .5602, RN oversight, manager qualifications, training hours and insurance minimums were not verified [S52]. The exact Construction fee is also unconfirmed (about $225 per home from a low-resolution slide). A requirement stricter than the model's would lower margins. Check the current rule text before signing a lease.
- **Cost-cap and policy uncertainty.** The waiver cost cap is stated as both $184,000 and $135,000 on the same NC Medicaid page [S8]. The effect of Appendix K flexibility sunsets was not verified.
- **Resident-income risk.** Room and board depends on each resident's SSI or earnings [S24]. Medicaid does not pay it [S15][S16], and Special Assistance eligibility must be checked for each resident with the county DSS [S25]. A $750 charge leaves about $244 of personal money for an SSI-only resident.
- **Concentration risk.** One LME/MCO region means one payer. A single home with six residents loses about 17% of revenue with each vacancy.
- **Cost-estimate risk.** Most non-wage costs (rent, insurance, accreditation, workers' compensation at 4.0%, benefits) are operator estimates. The NCRB workers' compensation class rate was not retrieved [S43].
sections.recommendations:
1. **Do not open a single 4-bed home or an all-Level-1 home.** Both lose money at real rates (-$5,715 and -$2,771 per month). The Level 3/4 home also loses (-$2,122) with two awake staff. The practical single-home option is one 6-bed home serving Level 2/3 residents, which earns about $1,368 per month, not enough to pay an operator who is also working in the home.
2. **Target three licensed 6-bed homes with Level 2/3 residents as the destination.** This is the profit-leading configuration: about $6,636 per month (5.7%), break-even at 84.5% occupancy, first profit in month 8, and about $408,323 of cash. Get there in stages. Open one home, reach 90% occupancy, then add the second (about $4,002 per month at 12 residents), and only then the third. Opening homes sequentially needs less cash than the modeled ramp-up deficit, which staffs all homes from month 1.
3. **Before leasing anything, get written answers from your LME/MCO.** Ask for its Residential Supports rate schedule by level, the assignment criteria for Levels 1–4, whether the $7.68 DCW add-on is already included in the rates, and whether Residential Supports is subject to EVV [S17][S18]. Also ask for the letter of support and for evidence of local need for supervised living beds [S3][S51]. Choose the LME/MCO region with the best documented rates.
4. **Start accreditation early.** Get quotes now from the accreditors your LME/MCO and the NCTracks Provider Permission Matrix accept for Residential Supports, since accreditation is required before you can enroll [S9]. Confirm with the LME/MCO how accreditation, license and contracting are sequenced.
5. **Budget wages at the sourced level, not $17.00.** Use about $18.49 per hour as the planning case [S32], and add an overtime/relief allowance for 24/7 coverage. At that wage the three-home model is roughly break-even (about $200 per month), so margin must come from higher occupancy, Level 3 residents or the DCW add-on, not from cutting required costs. File the DCW attestation immediately [S11][S18].
6. **Protect occupancy.** Break-even is 84.5% and the conservative case is 85%. Build relationships with LME/MCO care coordinators, waiver families and institutional transition teams [S48] so beds are not empty between residents. Pre-qualify residents and their guardians before you hire staff.
7. **Lock down unverified rule requirements.** Read the full 10A NCAC 27G .5602 staffing rule (ratio and overnight paragraphs), the RN rules, manager qualifications and training hours, and confirm the Construction fee with DHSR [S5]. Add the actual costs to your model. Get liability and workers' compensation quotes (workers' compensation is modeled at 4.0%, an estimate).
8. **Hold cash for the delay.** Plan on at least 8–10 weeks of construction review, more if a code interpretation is needed [S4][S5], up to six months for program review [S3] and payroll before licensure [S4]. Reserve at least the single-home figure of $132,963 per first home, and more for multiple homes, plus a contingency for slow fill.
9. **Stay compliant from day one.** Keep staff checks (criminal record and HCPR) and in-person CPR and medication training current [S5], renew the license annually before December 31 [S6], and track room-and-board charges against each resident's income [S24].

checklist.task: Confirm the pathway: licensed Supervised Living, 'C' designation, then Innovations Residential Supports
checklist.instructions: Adult I/DD group homes are licensed by DHSR Mental Health Licensure under G.S. 122C and 10A NCAC 27G .5600 (the 'C' designation covers adults whose primary diagnosis is a developmental disability). Medicaid pays for services separately, as NC Innovations Waiver Residential Supports through an LME/MCO Tailored Plan. You need both the license and the Medicaid enrollment and contract. Read the .5601 scope rule before committing to a business plan.

checklist.task: Understand when a license is mandatory and the penalty for operating without one
checklist.instructions: A supervised living facility must be licensed if it serves two or more adults (or one or more minors). Operating a licensable facility without a license is a Class H felony with a $1,000 per day fine. NC Medicaid's bulletin says an unlicensed supervised living home may serve only one adult. Do not place two or more residents before the license is issued.

checklist.task: Decide home size within the 6-client cap
checklist.instructions: A supervised living facility serving clients with developmental disabilities may serve no more than six clients. The 7-or-more-bed fee tier therefore does not apply to adult I/DD homes. CMS describes these homes as group homes of under seven beds. Note that NCDHHS counts group homes of fewer than four residents as community-based settings in its transition reporting, which matters if you target transitions from institutions.

checklist.task: Choose the population and keep minors and adults separate
checklist.instructions: Adults and minors may not live in the same facility. This bundle covers adult I/DD homes ('C' designation). If you later want to serve minors, that is a separate licensed facility.

checklist.task: Form the legal entity (LLC)
checklist.instructions: File Articles of Organization with the NC Secretary of State. A secondary guide lists the filing fee at $125 ($128 online with the card fee). Confirm the current fee on the Secretary of State site. Use the same exact legal name on every later application (DHSR, NCTracks, LME/MCO, accreditation, bank).

checklist.task: Calendar the LLC annual report
checklist.instructions: A secondary guide states NC LLCs file an annual report each year by April 15 with a $200 fee. The model carries $16.67 per month. Verify the fee and due date with the Secretary of State.

checklist.task: Decide tax treatment and check franchise tax exposure
checklist.instructions: A secondary source says LLCs taxed as partnerships do not owe NC franchise tax. An LLC that elects corporate treatment owes at least $200 per year ($1.50 per $1,000 of tax base). Ask your CPA before electing S-corp or C-corp status.

checklist.task: Obtain a federal EIN and open a business bank account
checklist.instructions: Apply free at irs.gov; the EIN is issued online immediately. Keep the confirmation letter. You will need it for NCTracks, accreditation and payroll. Open a separate operating account for the business.

checklist.task: Register as an employer with the NC Division of Employment Security
checklist.instructions: Register for unemployment insurance. The 2026 standard beginning (new employer) rate is 1.000% on a taxable wage base of $34,200; the maximum rate for experienced employers is 5.76%. Also register for NC withholding with the Department of Revenue and obtain a federal payroll account.

checklist.task: Arrange workers' compensation coverage
checklist.instructions: Get quotes from an NC broker for a residential care/group home class. The class rate was not retrieved from the NCRB 4/1/2026 loss-cost filing, so the model's 4.0% is an operator estimate. Check the NC Rate Bureau filings and your broker's quote before finalizing the budget.
checklist.cite: NC Rate Bureau workers' compensation filings

checklist.task: Obtain liability, property and auto insurance
checklist.instructions: No required minimum for supervised living homes was verified. Get quotes for general and professional liability, property, abuse/molestation if offered, and hired/non-owned auto. The model assumes about $400-$450 per home per month, which is an operator estimate. Accreditors and LME/MCOs may set their own minimums.

checklist.task: Check employer hiring compliance (E-Verify)
checklist.instructions: A secondary payroll guide says E-Verify is mandatory at 25 or more employees. A multi-home agency can cross that line. Confirm with the NC Department of Labor and set up Form I-9 procedures from the first hire.

checklist.task: Confirm wage floor and budget wages above it
checklist.instructions: The NC minimum wage is $7.25 per hour (secondary guide; local ordinances preempted). The model uses $17.00 per hour for direct support, an operator estimate. Sourced proxies run higher: NC CNA median about $18.49 and Raleigh-Cary personal care and service group mean $19.29. At $18.49 the default three-home model drops to about break-even, so budget for the higher wage.

checklist.task: Identify the LME/MCO Tailored Plan for the county where the home will be
checklist.instructions: There are four LME/MCOs (Alliance Health, Partners Health Management, Trillium Health Resources, Vaya Health), with one per county. The LME/MCO for your county issues the letter of support, administers Innovations services and pays you. Rates and contracting differ by plan, so choose the county with this in mind.

checklist.task: Contact the LME/MCO and request a letter of support
checklist.instructions: All residential providers other than ICF/IID must obtain an LME/MCO letter of support to accompany the DHSR application. Contact the LME/MCO network team early, describe the population, location and bed count, and ask for the process and timeline. The timeline is not published; plan for weeks to months.

checklist.task: Ask the LME/MCO about local need for supervised living beds
checklist.instructions: The LME determines the need for additional supervised living beds in its area under Subchapter G, and the rules escalate to DMH/DD/SAS if none exists. Ask whether your county is accepting new group home providers and in which levels of support.

checklist.task: Review waitlist and slot data for the demand case
checklist.instructions: NCDHHS reports 20,150 people remaining on the Innovations waitlist (Jul-Sep 2025), up from 18,457, with only 106 removed in the quarter and 14,736 approved active slots. No new slots were approved for FY2025-26. This shows demand but not referrals to your home. The dashboard does not forecast when people receive services. Check the official dashboard for the latest quarter.

checklist.task: Understand the referral channels
checklist.instructions: NCDHHS reports the Innovations Waiver (most often through Money Follows the Person) is the primary funding source for institutional transitions, and that people planning transitions most often want ICFs and group homes. Guardian objections are the leading reason people do not begin planning. Build relationships with LME/MCO care coordinators and transition teams. No referral is guaranteed to a new home.

checklist.task: Get the current Residential Supports rate sheet from your LME/MCO
checklist.instructions: Innovations services are managed by Tailored Plans and are outside the published state fee schedule. The only 2026 schedule retrieved is Alliance Health's (effective 10/1/2026): Level 1 $158.47, Level 2 $208.72, Level 3 $218.10, Level 4 $228.62 per day, subject to LME/MCO funding. Ask your plan for its rates, level definitions and how a resident is assigned a level. Re-run the P&L with those rates.
checklist.cite: Alliance Health FY27 Standard Rate Schedule

checklist.task: Ask whether the DCW add-on is already in your plan's per diem
checklist.instructions: The S.L. 2026-41 code table lists a $7.68 per diem direct care worker add-on for Residential Supports (effective 10/1/2026, retroactive to 7/1/2026). Providers must submit an attestation to receive it. Whether it is already inside the Alliance schedule is not verified. The model does not stack it. Confirm with your LME/MCO before counting it.

checklist.task: Check the status of the 3% rate reduction
checklist.instructions: A 2025 SPA notice said Innovations services managed by Tailored Plans were to receive a 3% reduction effective 10/1/2025. Whether it remains in effect in 2026 is not verified. Ask the LME/MCO whether its current schedule reflects it.

checklist.task: Review the Innovations benefit plan for service interactions and limits
checklist.instructions: Trillium's 2026-2027 benefit plan says a member receiving Residential Supports may not also receive several other services (Home Modifications, Community Living and Supports, Respite and others). It also caps combined community networking, day supports and supported employment at 40 hours per week for adults in residential settings. Confirm each limit with your own LME/MCO.

checklist.task: Verify the waiver is active and note its cost cap
checklist.instructions: The NC Innovations Waiver is a 1915(c) waiver (No. 0423.R04.00), reported as renewed July 1, 2024 through June 30, 2029. NC Medicaid's page states a $184,000 per waiver year cap under Appendix K, though other passages still cite $135,000. Treat the cap as unconfirmed and ask the LME/MCO how it affects residents with high support needs.

checklist.phase: PHASE 3 — SITE SELECTION, ZONING & PHYSICAL PLANT
checklist.task: Select a home that can meet the physical plant rules
checklist.instructions: Single bedrooms must be at least 100 sq ft; double bedrooms at least 160 sq ft; no more than two clients may share a bedroom. At least one full bathroom is required per five or fewer persons, counting staff and their family, so a 6-resident home needs at least two full baths. Walk every candidate home with these dimensions before signing a lease.

checklist.phase: PHASE 3 — SITE SELECTION, ZONING & PHYSICAL PLANT
checklist.task: Check egress requirements
checklist.instructions: Facilities with 4 to 6 clients, or two-story homes, must meet the NC Building Code rule that each normally occupied story has two remotely located exits. Budget for added exits or window/door modifications. Confirm details with the DHSR Construction Section.

checklist.phase: PHASE 3 — SITE SELECTION, ZONING & PHYSICAL PLANT
checklist.task: Avoid manufactured homes for more than three residents
checklist.instructions: Manufactured or mobile homes may serve only three or fewer residents, and only under supervised living or community respite. A 6-bed model needs a site-built home.

checklist.phase: PHASE 3 — SITE SELECTION, ZONING & PHYSICAL PLANT
checklist.task: Obtain local zoning approval
checklist.instructions: Providers of day, outpatient and residential services need zoning approval, which is submitted with the DHSR application. Contact the city or county planning office, describe the use, and get written approval. Do not sign a lease before you know the use is allowed.

checklist.phase: PHASE 3 — SITE SELECTION, ZONING & PHYSICAL PLANT
checklist.task: Get landlord consent for group home use
checklist.instructions: If leasing, put the group home use, the zoning approval contingency and the right to make required modifications in writing. Rent is a fixed cost whether beds are full or not; the model uses $2,800 per 4-5 bedroom home as an operator estimate. No sourced local rent benchmark was found, so get local quotes.

checklist.phase: PHASE 3 — SITE SELECTION, ZONING & PHYSICAL PLANT
checklist.task: Call the Construction Section Help Desk
checklist.instructions: Ask about project review fee, required plans, fire/life safety items and local building/fire inspections for your exact address. Phone (919) 855-3893. The construction fee amount was not retrieved, so budget is a placeholder.

checklist.phase: PHASE 3 — SITE SELECTION, ZONING & PHYSICAL PLANT
checklist.task: Make required modifications and furnish the home
checklist.instructions: Complete bedroom, bathroom and egress work. The facility must be completely furnished and ready to open before an initial license is issued, with staff in place. Budget about $7,000 per home for furniture and housewares (operator estimate). Smoking is prohibited inside licensed facilities by any person living or employed there; post signage.

checklist.phase: PHASE 3 — SITE SELECTION, ZONING & PHYSICAL PLANT
checklist.task: Install safety equipment
checklist.instructions: Equip each home with smoke alarms, fire extinguishers, first aid supplies and bedroom hardware appropriate to residents. Specific equipment counts come from the DHSR Construction review and local fire inspection; confirm before purchase. Budget is about $1,500 per home (operator estimate).

checklist.task: Download the Initial Mental Health Licensure Application Packet
checklist.instructions: Get the packet from the DHSR Mental Health Licensure & Certification website. Read the establish-a-service page first. Mail address: 2718 Mail Service Center, Raleigh, NC 27699-2718. Applications are not complete until all items are included.

checklist.task: Include the LME/MCO letter of support with the application
checklist.instructions: The letter is required for residential applicants other than ICF/IID (G.S. 122C-23.1). Attach it to the packet. Without it the application is incomplete.

checklist.task: Include zoning approval and all required packet items
checklist.instructions: Submit the local zoning approval and the other attachments the packet lists. The packet states to include the initial licensure fee upon submitting all items. Make a copy of the full submission for your records.

checklist.task: Pay the initial license fee with the application
checklist.instructions: Non-ICF/IID facilities with 6 or fewer beds pay $350 base and $0 per bed. The 7+ bed tier ($525 + $19 per bed) does not apply to adult I/DD homes capped at 6. One license is needed per home. The license will not be issued until the fee is paid.

checklist.task: Pay the Construction project review fee before review
checklist.instructions: The construction fee must be returned and paid before a review or initial inspection can be done. The amount by bed count was not retrieved; confirm with the Construction Section Help Desk and pay promptly because it holds up the review.

checklist.task: Track the review timeline
checklist.instructions: After the packet is submitted and the fee paid, DHSR sends it to the Construction Section. The establish page says to expect construction review in about 10-12 weeks; a February 2026 DHSR deck says 8-10 weeks. Plan for the longer figure. Applicants have six months to complete the program review, after which the application can be rescinded or denied.

checklist.task: Respond to DHSR comments immediately
checklist.instructions: Incomplete or deficient items slow the process and the six-month program review window keeps running. Designate one person to respond, and keep a log of every submission and date.

checklist.task: Name a qualified professional (QP) and confirm credentials
checklist.instructions: A qualified professional holds a license, provisional license, certificate, registration or permit from the governing board of a human service profession (10A NCAC 27G .0104). Manager and QP requirements for supervised living were not fully verified, so confirm what the rule requires for your home with DHSR before hiring.

checklist.task: Plan for annual license renewal
checklist.instructions: Licenses must be renewed annually and expire at the end of the calendar year (December 31). The renewal fee amount was not verified; the model assumes it equals the $350 initial fee. Calendar the renewal for each home.

checklist.task: Confirm the current staffing rules before building schedules
checklist.instructions: The .5600 staffing ratio and awake-overnight requirements were not retrieved. A 2018 DHHS report describes at least one staff per six individuals, but that is not confirmed as current. Read the current rule text for your designation and ask DHSR or your LME/MCO. The model uses 973 to 1,460 coverage hours per home per month as operator estimates.

checklist.task: Run a criminal record check on every staff member
checklist.instructions: All staff members must undergo a Criminal Record Check within 180 days of the application review. Start the checks while the application is under review so they remain current.

checklist.task: Complete the Health Care Personnel Registry (HCPR) check for every staff member
checklist.instructions: The HCPR check must be completed within 90 days of the licensure review. Keep results in each personnel file.

checklist.task: Hire all staff before the initial license is issued
checklist.instructions: Staff must be in place and the facility completely furnished and ready to open before an initial license is issued. Budget two to three weeks of paid pre-opening labor (operator estimate $8,000-$24,000 including training and checks).

checklist.task: Arrange your own staff training because DHSR provides none
checklist.instructions: DHSR does not provide any personnel training. You must source trainers and records for every required course. Verify the required topics and hours in the rule text and with your LME/MCO and accreditor; annual hours were not verified.

checklist.task: Use in-person CPR courses
checklist.instructions: Online-only CPR courses are not accepted. Book an in-person or blended course with a hands-on skills component for all staff.

checklist.task: Complete in-person medication administration training for all staff
checklist.instructions: If the facility stores or administers medication, all staff must receive training. It must be in person and delivered by a qualified trainer (RN, pharmacist or other legally qualified trainer). Schedule before the licensure review.

checklist.task: Retain a registered nurse consultant
checklist.instructions: The model carries 1.5-2.5 RN hours per resident per month at about $40.56 per hour (secondary summary of BLS May 2025 NC median RN wage). Current RN oversight requirements were not verified, so confirm with DHSR and your LME/MCO. The same RN can serve as your qualified medication trainer if licensed appropriately.

checklist.task: Plan recruitment around the direct support professional shortage
checklist.instructions: NCDHHS states NC faces a critical shortage of DSPs. In Jul-Sep 2025 626,791 authorized CLS units went unused because of lack of provider or staff availability. Budget for turnover and overtime, offer wages at or above the sourced proxies, and keep a bench of trained relief staff.

checklist.task: Set up payroll and employee file systems
checklist.instructions: Use a payroll service, collect I-9 and W-4 forms, and keep background check, HCPR, training and competency records in each file for the DHSR and accreditation reviews. Model assumes $600-$900 per month for accounting, payroll and legal (operator estimate).

checklist.task: Obtain national accreditation before enrolling as a Residential Supports provider
checklist.instructions: NC Medicaid requires one of COA, CQL, JCAHO or CARF for Residential Supports providers enrolling under the Innovations taxonomy after April 20, 2026. Contact the accreditors for quotes and timelines. Fees were not found; the model assumes $6,000-$15,000 initial and $500-$700 per month amortized, both operator estimates.

checklist.task: Enroll in NC Medicaid through NCTracks
checklist.instructions: Complete the provider enrollment application. Group-home-specific taxonomy and enrollment steps for Residential Supports were not found, so confirm with NCTracks and your LME/MCO. A vendor blog reported clean applications processed in about 11.76 days in June 2026; treat that as a secondary, non-guaranteed figure.

checklist.task: Pay the NC Medicaid application fee
checklist.instructions: NC assesses a $100 provider application fee on enrollment, re-enrollment and revalidation. It is charged at initial enrollment and every five years at re-credentialing.

checklist.task: Find out whether the federal enrollment fee applies
checklist.instructions: The federal Medicaid enrollment fee is $750 for CY2026, payable when applicable depending on provider type. Whether it applies to a Residential Supports group home provider was not confirmed. Ask NCTracks before paying so you do not overpay or delay enrollment.

checklist.task: Apply to join the LME/MCO provider network and sign the contract
checklist.instructions: The LME/MCO administers waiver services and oversees the provider network. Ask about credentialing steps, contract terms, claims submission, authorization process, audit rules and payment timing. Contract with every LME/MCO whose members you want to serve.

checklist.task: File the DCW rate increase attestation with the LME/MCO
checklist.instructions: To receive the SFY 2027 Innovations DCW rate increase, providers must submit an attestation to their LME/MCO before payment. LME/MCOs report usage to NC Medicaid by the revised date of December 1, 2027. Set up payroll tracking so you can show the funds went to direct care worker wages.

checklist.task: Confirm whether EVV applies to your residential service
checklist.instructions: NC Medicaid requires EVV for certain HCBS including some Innovations services, and Tailored Plans use HHAeXchange as their designated EVV vendor. The sources reviewed name Community Living and Supports and Supported Living but not Residential Supports. Ask your LME/MCO in writing and complete HHAeXchange onboarding if required.

checklist.task: Review the Innovations waiver service definition and room-and-board exclusion
checklist.instructions: Payments for Residential Supports do not include room and board, and Medicaid does not pay room and board. Only a staff differential may be covered during a roommate search. Read the service definition so your billing, service plans and documentation match it.
checklist.cite: NC Medicaid special bulletin; Innovations FAQ

checklist.phase: PHASE 7 — POLICIES, RESIDENT SERVICES & RESIDENT INTAKE
checklist.task: Write the policies and procedures manual
checklist.instructions: Cover client rights, medication management, emergency and fire procedures, incident reporting, abuse and neglect, and staff training. Budget $2,000-$6,000 if you use a consultant (operator estimate). Align with accreditor standards so one manual serves both.

checklist.phase: PHASE 7 — POLICIES, RESIDENT SERVICES & RESIDENT INTAKE
checklist.task: Build the medication system
checklist.instructions: Set up medication storage, MARs, staff authorization and pharmacy relationships. Everyone who stores or administers medication must have the in-person training before the review.

checklist.phase: PHASE 7 — POLICIES, RESIDENT SERVICES & RESIDENT INTAKE
checklist.task: Create the resident intake and admission packet
checklist.instructions: Include a residency agreement, room-and-board agreement, rights notice, emergency contacts, guardian information and consent forms. Residents are placed through the LME/MCO choice-list process and authorizations, so ask the plan how referrals and authorizations are handled.

checklist.phase: PHASE 7 — POLICIES, RESIDENT SERVICES & RESIDENT INTAKE
checklist.task: Set a compliant room-and-board charge
checklist.instructions: The 2026 SSI federal benefit rate is $994 per month for an individual. The model assumes $750 per month room and board, an operator estimate that leaves about $244 for personal needs. Verify each resident's income and the LME/MCO's rules. Do not charge more than the resident can pay.

checklist.phase: PHASE 7 — POLICIES, RESIDENT SERVICES & RESIDENT INTAKE
checklist.task: Evaluate State/County Special Assistance as a room-and-board source
checklist.instructions: Special Assistance is a cash supplement for residents of approved residential facilities, including group homes, and the facility must accept the state rate. Eligibility is age 65+ or disability. A secondary guide lists a $1,397 base maximum; the official rate was not verified and whether your home qualifies was not verified. Ask the county DSS.

checklist.phase: PHASE 7 — POLICIES, RESIDENT SERVICES & RESIDENT INTAKE
checklist.task: Set up resident funds and personal-needs accounting
checklist.instructions: Keep a separate ledger for each resident's money (SSI, SSDI, earnings), with receipts and a documented policy. Auditors and LME/MCO monitors will ask for it.

checklist.phase: PHASE 7 — POLICIES, RESIDENT SERVICES & RESIDENT INTAKE
checklist.task: Arrange transportation for community participation
checklist.instructions: Budget a vehicle per home (model $800 per month, operator estimate). Verify driver licensing, auto insurance and NC financial responsibility requirements, which were not verified here.

checklist.phase: PHASE 7 — POLICIES, RESIDENT SERVICES & RESIDENT INTAKE
checklist.task: Set up billing, authorization and records software
checklist.instructions: Track LME/MCO authorizations, daily attendance and claims. Model assumes $35 per resident per month (operator estimate). Choose software that can export to the LME/MCO claims portal and supports EVV if required.

checklist.task: Pass the Construction Section review and site inspection
checklist.instructions: After the construction fee is paid, DHSR Construction reviews the project and may visit the site. Correct any items quickly. Have local building and fire clearances ready if requested.

checklist.task: Complete the program review within six months
checklist.instructions: DHSR gives the applicant six months to complete the program review. After that the application can be rescinded or denied. Have policies, staff files, training certificates and the furnished home ready before the visit.

checklist.task: Confirm all staff files are complete before the licensure review
checklist.instructions: Check that each file has the criminal record check (within 180 days), HCPR check (within 90 days), CPR, medication training and QP credentials where applicable. Missing items delay licensure.

checklist.task: Do not admit two or more adults until the license is issued
checklist.instructions: Opening early exposes you to the Class H felony penalty and a $1,000 per day fine. Wait for the written license.

checklist.task: Sequence licensure, accreditation and Medicaid enrollment so billing can start
checklist.instructions: Medicaid pays only after the license, accreditation, NCTracks enrollment and LME/MCO contract are in place and a resident is authorized. Start accreditation and enrollment while DHSR review is underway. Model the cash gap; the three-home model needs about $408,000 in cash through ramp-up.

checklist.task: Open homes one at a time if cash is limited
checklist.instructions: The model staffs every home from month one, so opening and filling homes sequentially needs less cash. The default three-home model first turns profitable around month 8 and needs about 84.5% occupancy to break even.

checklist.task: Notify the LME/MCO that you are open and ready for referrals
checklist.instructions: Send the license copy and bed availability to the care coordination and network teams. Ask to be listed on the choice list.

checklist.task: Bill the correct per diem codes and levels
checklist.instructions: Alliance's schedule lists H2016 (Level 1), T2014 (Level 2), T2020 (Level 3) and H2016 HI (Level 4). Confirm codes and modifiers with your own LME/MCO. Bill only for days of service authorized.

checklist.task: Track occupancy and break-even weekly
checklist.instructions: The default three-home Level 2/3 model earns about $6,636 per month (5.7% margin) at 90% occupancy and breaks even near 84.5%. A single home with Level 1 residents needs about 99% occupancy, so do not rely on it. Monitor vacancies and speed up admissions.

checklist.task: Stress-test wages
checklist.instructions: At $18.49 per hour (NC CNA median proxy) instead of $17.00, the default three-home model falls to about $200 per month profit at 90% occupancy. Rerun your own P&L at the wages you actually pay and the rates your LME/MCO actually publishes.

checklist.task: Build a reserve for rate changes and delayed payments
checklist.instructions: Alliance states its Innovations rates are subject to change based on LME/MCO funding. Keep several months of operating reserve and watch NC Medicaid and LME/MCO notices.

checklist.task: Keep documentation to support claims and audits
checklist.instructions: Retain service notes, attendance, authorizations and staff time records so claims can withstand LME/MCO post-payment review. EVV data, if applicable, must match claims.

checklist.task: File required tax reports on time
checklist.instructions: File quarterly payroll and unemployment reports, the LLC annual report (April 15 per secondary guide) and annual tax returns. Missed filings can affect good standing needed for contracts.

checklist.task: Prepare for annual reviews and complaint inspections
checklist.instructions: DHSR performs complaint resolution, annual reviews and inspections of each group home. Findings can result in license suspension or revocation. Run internal audits quarterly against the 27G .5600 rules and past DHSR statements of deficiencies, which are posted publicly.

checklist.task: Renew each license annually before December 31
checklist.instructions: Licenses expire at the end of the calendar year. Calendar the renewal and fee for each home. Renewal amount was not verified.

checklist.task: Maintain accreditation and re-credential in NCTracks
checklist.instructions: Keep the accreditation current and complete NCTracks revalidation. The $100 NC fee recurs every five years and the federal fee applies when applicable.

checklist.task: Keep staff background checks and training current
checklist.instructions: Run criminal record and HCPR checks on every new hire and keep CPR and medication training current. DHSR does not train, so build your own annual schedule.

checklist.task: Give DHSR 30 days' written notice before any change of ownership
checklist.instructions: The current licensee must notify DHSR in writing at least 30 days before a planned change of ownership. The new owner may not operate until licensed. Change-of-ownership fees were not verified.

checklist.task: Monitor rule and rate changes
checklist.instructions: Watch NC Medicaid bulletins, LME/MCO rate schedules, the DCW attestation and reporting dates, accreditation requirements and any pending changes to 10A NCAC 27G .5600. No proposed amendment was found at the time of research.

checklist.task: Stay current on waitlist and slot data
checklist.instructions: The NCDHHS Innovations Waitlist Dashboard is refreshed quarterly and does not forecast when people will receive services. Use it to time expansion into additional homes.
